TECHNOVA 
Grievance_and_Escalation_Procedure 2026 
Effective Date: June 15, 2026 
Version: 2.0 
Approved By: Chief Human Resources Officer (CHRO). 

1.0 Our Commitment to a Fair Workplace 
1.1 Purpose and Philosophy 
At Technova, we are dedicated to fostering a positive, respectful, and productive work environment 
where every employee feels valued and heard. This Grievance and Escalation Procedure is designed 
to provide a clear, fair, and consistent framework for raising and resolving workplace concerns. 
Our philosophy is that open communication and early resolution are the most effective ways to 
address issues. We believe that by providing a structured and transparent process, we can address 
conflicts constructively, reinforce our company values, and ensure that all employees are treated 
with dignity and respect. This procedure serves as a core tool to help us uphold our commitment to a 
healthy workplace culture. 
1.2 Scope of This Policy 
This policy applies to all regular full-time and part-time employees of Technova. It covers any 
concern, problem, or complaint that an employee may have regarding their work, the work 
environment, or their employment relationship. This includes, but is not limited to, issues related to 
working conditions, treatment by managers or colleagues, and the application of company policies. 
1.3 Core Principles 
This procedure is founded on four essential principles that guide our approach at every stage: 
• 
Confidentiality: All grievances will be handled with the utmost discretion. Information will 
only be shared with those who have a legitimate need to know in order to investigate and 
resolve the concern. 
• 
Non-Retaliation: Technova has a strict zero-tolerance policy for retaliation. No employee will 
face adverse action, harassment, or discrimination for raising a grievance in good faith or for 
participating in an investigation. Any act of retaliation is a serious violation of company policy 
and will result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination. 
• 
Impartiality and Fairness: Every grievance will be investigated and reviewed objectively and 
impartially. Decisions will be based on a thorough and fair assessment of the facts. All parties 
involved will have an opportunity to present their side of the story. 
• 
Timeliness: We are committed to addressing all concerns promptly. This policy outlines 
specific timelines for each stage of the process to ensure that grievances are resolved 
without unnecessary delay. 
1.4 What is a Grievance?

A grievance is a formal complaint raised by an employee concerning a work-related issue that they 
believe is unfair, unjust, or in violation of company policy or legal standards. Examples of issues that 
may form the basis of a grievance include: 
• 
Perceived unfair or inequitable treatment. 
• 
Bullying, harassment, or discrimination. 
• 
Concerns about health and safety in the workplace. 
• 
Disputes over the interpretation or application of HR policies like leave and work hours. 
• 
Violations of the company's Code of Conduct. 
1.5 What is Not Covered by This Procedure? 
This procedure is not intended to address every type of workplace disagreement. The following 
issues are typically handled through separate, specific processes: 
• 
Disciplinary Action: Appeals against formal disciplinary warnings or actions. 
• 
Termination of Employment: Decisions related to the formal termination of employment. 
• 
Compensation Decisions: Issues related to salary, bonus amounts, or equity awards, which 
are managed through the annual compensation review process. 
• 
Performance Feedback: Disagreements with performance ratings or feedback received 
during a performance review. 
• 
Whistleblowing: Reports of illegal activity, financial malpractice, or serious dangers to public 
health, which should be raised under the company's Whistleblower Policy. 
2.0 Roles and Responsibilities 
A successful grievance process relies on the active and responsible participation of all parties 
involved. 
2.1 The Employee 
• 
To attempt, where appropriate, to resolve concerns informally at the earliest opportunity. 
• 
To raise formal grievances in a timely and factual manner, providing all relevant information. 
• 
To cooperate fully with any investigation. 
• 
To maintain strict confidentiality throughout the entire process. 
2.2 The Manager 
• 
To foster an environment where employees feel comfortable raising concerns. 
• 
To listen actively and take all coworker concerns seriously. 
• 
To make genuine efforts to resolve issues informally and promptly. 
• 
To participate constructively in formal investigations when required. 
• 
To uphold the core principles of confidentiality and non-retaliation.

2.3 The Human Resources (HR) Department 
• 
To act as an impartial steward of the grievance procedure. 
• 
To provide advice and support to both employees and managers throughout the process. 
• 
To ensure all formal grievances are properly documented, investigated, and resolved in 
accordance with this policy. 
• 
To appoint trained and completely impartial investigators. 
• 
To maintain secure records of all grievance proceedings. 
2.4 The Grievance Committee 
A formal Grievance Committee may be convened to hear appeals. The Committee typically consists 
of a senior HR leader, a senior leader from a neutral department, and another impartial manager. 
The Committee's role is to provide a final, objective review of the grievance and the initial decision. 
3.0 Informal Grievance Resolution 
3.1 The Value of Informal Resolution 
We strongly encourage employees to try and resolve concerns informally before initiating a formal 
grievance. Many workplace issues arise from simple misunderstandings or miscommunications and 
can often be resolved quickly and effectively through direct conversation. An informal approach can 
help preserve working relationships and find mutually agreeable solutions without the need for a 
lengthy formal process. 
3.2 Step-by-Step Informal Process 
• 
Reflect and Prepare: Before approaching anyone, take a moment to clearly identify the 
issue. What specifically is the problem, and what is your desired outcome? 
• 
Speak with Your Manager: Your direct manager is usually the best first point of contact. 
Schedule a private meeting to discuss your concerns openly and professionally. 
• 
Alternative Contact: If you are not comfortable speaking with your manager, or if your 
concern is about your manager, you can approach their manager or an HR Business Partner 
for an informal discussion. 
• 
Discussion and Agreement: The goal of the informal discussion is to reach a shared 
understanding and agree on a path forward, which could involve clarifying expectations, 
changing a process, or simply having a constructive dialogue. 
3.3 The Role of Mediation 
In some cases, a facilitated conversation with a neutral third party can be helpful. HR can act as an 
impartial mediator to help employees and managers discuss their issues and find common ground. 
Mediation is a voluntary process aimed at achieving a mutually acceptable resolution. 
3.4 Informal Resolution Case Study: Recognizing Contributions 
• 
Scenario: Alex, a graphic designer, feels that his colleague, Ben, is consistently taking credit 
for his ideas in team meetings, which is causing friction and demotivating Alex.

• 
Action: Instead of immediately filing a complaint, Alex schedules a one-on-one meeting with 
his manager, Sarah. He calmly explains the situation with specific examples and states that 
his desired outcome is fair recognition. Sarah listens, validates his feelings, and agrees to 
observe team dynamics. She also has a separate coaching conversation with Ben about 
teamwork and acknowledging contributors. 
• 
Outcome: In subsequent meetings, Sarah asks for input from all team members, and Ben 
becomes more mindful of giving credit. Alex feels heard and respected, and the issue is 
resolved without damaging the working relationship. 
4.0 Formal Grievance Procedure 
4.1 When to Initiate a Formal Grievance 
A formal grievance should be initiated when an attempt at informal resolution has been 
unsuccessful, the nature of the grievance is too serious for an informal approach, or the grievance is 
against your direct manager and you are not comfortable addressing it with them informally. 
4.2 Step-by-Step Formal Process 
• 
Step 1: Filing a Formal Grievance: To begin the formal process, the employee must submit a 
written grievance to the HR department using the official Grievance Form. The submission 
should include a detailed description of the event, relevant dates, locations, witnesses, 
supporting evidence, and your desired outcome. 
• 
Step 2: Acknowledgment and Assessment: HR will acknowledge receipt of the formal 
grievance in writing within two (2) working days. HR will then conduct an initial assessment 
and appoint an impartial investigator. 
• 
Step 3: Formal Investigation: The investigator will conduct a thorough and objective 
investigation, interviewing the grievant, the respondent, and relevant witnesses, while 
reviewing documents like emails and company records privately. 
• 
Step 4: Grievance Meeting: After the investigation is complete, a formal grievance meeting 
will be scheduled and chaired by an uninvolved manager. The employee has the right to be 
accompanied at this meeting by a work colleague or a certified trade union representative. 
• 
Step 5: Decision and Notification: Following the meeting, the chairperson will consider all 
the evidence and communicate the final decision and corrective remedies in writing, 
typically within five (5) working days. 
4.3 Target Timelines for the Formal Process 
• 
Acknowledgment of Grievance: 2 working days. 
• 
Completion of Investigation: 15 working days. 
• 
Grievance Meeting: Within 5 working days of investigation completion. 
• 
Written Decision: Within 5 working days of the meeting. 
4.4 Formal Process Case Study: Promotion Discrepancies

• 
Scenario: Maria, an employee in the finance department, believes she was overlooked for a 
promotion in favor of a less-qualified colleague, feeling it is a case of bias. She loses trust in 
her manager and files a formal grievance. 
• 
Action: Maria completes the Grievance Form, citing specific projects and performance 
metrics. HR acknowledges it within two days and assigns a senior HR specialist to investigate. 
The investigator interviews Maria, her manager, and the promoted colleague, and reviews 
interview notes and promotion criteria. A meeting is held, chaired by the Director of Finance, 
which Maria attends with a colleague for support. 
• 
Outcome: The investigation concludes that the selection process lacked clear, objective 
scoring, leading to the appearance of bias. The Director upholds part of the grievance, 
committing to a detailed development plan for Maria and a mandate for the department to 
implement a more structured promotion process. 
5.0 Escalation and Appeal Process 
5.1 The Right to Appeal 
If an employee is not satisfied with the outcome of the formal grievance procedure, they have the 
right to appeal the decision. An appeal is not a re-investigation of the grievance but a review of the 
original decision and the process used to reach it. 
5.2 Grounds for an Appeal 
An appeal may be submitted on one or more of the following grounds: 
• 
New evidence has come to light that was not available during the original investigation. 
• 
There was a significant flaw in the procedure followed, which may have affected the 
outcome. 
• 
The decision or the resulting action was not reasonable or proportionate based on the 
findings. 
5.3 How to Submit an Appeal 
An employee wishing to appeal must do so in writing to the HR department within five (5) working 
days of receiving the formal grievance decision. The written appeal must clearly state the specific 
grounds on which the appeal is being made. 
5.4 The Appeal Hearing and Final Decision 
The appeal will be heard by an Appeal Panel consisting of a senior leader not previously involved and 
the Grievance Committee. The employee will be invited to present their case and retains the right to 
be accompanied by a colleague or union representative. 
The decision of the Appeal Panel is final, and there is no further internal right of appeal. The final 
decision will be communicated to the employee in writing within five (5) working days of the appeal 
hearing. 
5.5 Appeal Process Case Study: Strengthening Remedies 
• 
Scenario: In the case above, Maria is not satisfied with the remedy offered, feeling a 
development plan alone does not address the core issue of bias in the promotion decision.

• 
Action: Maria submits a written appeal within five days. An Appeal Panel is convened, 
chaired by the company's Chief Human Resources Officer (CHRO). At the appeal hearing, 
Maria argues her case. 
• 
Outcome: The Appeal Panel reviews the case and agrees that the remedy should be 
strengthened. The panel's final decision includes a formal written apology and mandates that 
Maria be automatically included in the interview pool for the next relevant promotion 
opportunity. This decision is final. 
6.0 Handling Specific Types of Grievances 
6.1 Grievances Involving a Direct Manager 
If a grievance is about an employee's direct manager, the employee is not required to address it with 
them informally. The formal grievance should be submitted directly to the next level of management 
or to an HR Business Partner. 
6.2 Harassment, Bullying, or Discrimination 
Allegations of harassment, bullying, or discrimination are taken extremely seriously. These grievances 
will always be handled through the formal procedure and will be investigated by specially trained HR 
professionals or external investigators. These investigations are governed by the company's separate 
Anti-Harassment and Equal Employment Opportunity policies. 
6.3 Collective Grievances vs. Whistleblowing 
• 
Collective Grievances: If a group of employees shares the same grievance, they may submit 
it collectively. One or two employees should be nominated as spokespersons for the group to 
liaise with HR throughout the process. 
• 
Whistleblowing Distinction: A grievance typically relates to an employee's personal 
circumstances or treatment. A whistleblowing complaint involves reporting information that 
is in the public interest, such as criminal activity, corruption, or serious dangers, which 
should be raised under the company's separate Whistleblower Policy. 
7.0 Confidentiality and Data Protection 
7.1 Maintaining Confidentiality 
All individuals involved in a grievance procedure—the grievant, the respondent, witnesses, 
managers, and HR—are required to maintain strict confidentiality. Breaches of confidentiality can 
undermine the integrity of the process and may result in disciplinary action. 
7.2 Data Protection and Record-Keeping 
HR will create and maintain a confidential case file for each formal grievance. This file will be stored 
securely and separately from the employee's main personnel file. Access will be restricted strictly to 
authorized HR and legal personnel, and all records will be managed in compliance with data 
protection laws. 
8.0 Policy Review and Training 
8.1 Policy Review Framework

This policy will be reviewed by the HR department every two years, or more frequently if required by 
changes in legislation, to ensure it remains effective and fully compliant. 
8.2 Training and Awareness 
All managers will receive mandatory training on this policy and on their role in handling workplace 
concerns effectively and empathetically. The policy will be made available to all employees via the 
company's intranet, and it will be covered thoroughly during new hire orientation. 
9.0 Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 
Q1: Do I have to talk to my manager before filing a formal grievance? A: While we strongly 
encourage informal resolution first, you are not required to speak with your manager if you are 
uncomfortable doing so or if your grievance is about them. In that case, you can go directly to HR. 
Q2: Will filing a grievance negatively impact my career? A: Absolutely not. Our non-retaliation 
policy is strictly enforced. It is a serious violation of company policy to penalize an employee in any 
way for raising a concern in good faith. 
Q3: Can I remain anonymous when I file a grievance? A: Due to the need to conduct a thorough 
investigation, it is generally not possible to remain completely anonymous when filing a formal 
grievance. However, we will maintain confidentiality to the greatest extent possible. 
Q4: How long does the formal grievance process take? A: We aim to complete the entire formal 
process, from filing to decision, within approximately 25-30 working days. However, complex cases 
may take longer. 
Q5: Who can I bring with me to a grievance or appeal meeting? A: You have the right to be 
accompanied by a single individual who is a current work colleague or a certified trade union 
representative. They are there for support and are not permitted to answer questions on your behalf. 
Q6: What happens if my grievance is not upheld? A: If your grievance is not upheld, HR will still offer 
support and may suggest mediation or other actions to help repair working relationships and move 
forward constructively. 
Q7: Can I withdraw my grievance after I have filed it? A: Yes, you can withdraw your grievance at 
any stage by notifying HR in writing. However, in cases involving serious allegations, the company 
may be obligated to continue the investigation regardless. 
10.0 Formal Grievance Form Framework 
The official, downloadable Formal Grievance Form is securely hosted on our internal HR portal. For 
reference, the structured data input fields required for filing include: 
• 
Employee Details: Full Name, Employee ID, Department, Direct Manager's Name, and Date 
of Submission. 
• 
Section 1: Details of the Grievance: A detailed description of the grievance including specific 
facts, dates, times, locations, individuals involved, and names of any witnesses. 
• 
Section 2: Informal Resolution Attempts: A descriptive summary of any steps already taken 
to resolve the matter informally. 
• 
Section 3: Desired Resolution: A clear description of the specific outcome you are seeking to 
resolve the workplace concern.

• 
Section 4: Supporting Documentation: A list of all physical or digital documents (e.g., emails, 
files, messages) provided to support the filing. 
• 
Sign-off Block: Employee physical or electronic signature and date lines.
